findings.title: limitFunction drops every caller argument
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is declared as a zero-argument function and invokes the wrapped function as function_(), instead of forwarding ...arguments_ through the limiter.
findings.impact: Any caller using limitFunction with a parameterized function receives undefined arguments at runtime, while the TypeScript declaration advertises that the returned function accepts the original function arguments.
evidence: index.d.ts:133-136 declares limitFunction returns (...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>.
Focused runtime probe invoked limitFunction((a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1})("left", "right") and observed [undefined, undefined] (JSON output [null,null]).
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run a Node ESM probe that loads index.js with an in-memory yocto-queue stub, then await limitFunction((a, b) => [a, b], {concurrency: 1})("left", "right"); expected ["left", "right"], observed [undefined, undefined].

findings.title: limit.map omits indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call passes iterableIsArray ? index : undefined, so Sets, generators, and iterator inputs never receive the index promised by the API.
findings.impact: Consumers using limit.map with any non-array iterable cannot rely on the documented mapper index, breaking ordering or keying logic that works with Array.from semantics.
evidence: readme.md:78-84 says the mapper receives the item value and its index and is equivalent to Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index)).
index.js:107-112 only forwards index when Array.isArray(iterable) is true.
Focused runtime probe over new Set(["a", "b"]) returned ["a:undefined", "b:undefined"].
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run await pLimit(2).map(new Set(["a", "b"]), (value, index) => `${value}:${String(index)}`); expected ["a:0", "b:1"], observed ["a:undefined", "b:undefined"].

findings.title: Options-object usage enables rejectOnClear by default
findings.cause: When concurrency is an options object, destructuring defaults rejectOnClear to true even though the public contract documents the default as false.
findings.impact: Calling pLimit({concurrency: 1}) changes clearQueue() from leaving pending promises pending to rejecting them with AbortError, causing unexpected Promise.all failures for users who only switched to object syntax to pass concurrency.
evidence: readme.md:46-52 documents rejectOnClear as Type boolean, Default false.
Focused runtime probe with pLimit({concurrency: 1}) queued a pending task, called clearQueue(), and observed rejected:AbortError.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Create const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); queue one long task and one pending task; after await Promise.resolve(), call limit.clearQueue(); expected pending promise to remain pending under default false, observed AbortError rejection.

findings.title: Falsey non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation branch checks typeof rejectOnClear only when rejectOnClear is truthy, so values such as 0, null, or an empty string are accepted.
findings.impact: Invalid options are silently accepted and coerced into behavior, weakening the documented boolean contract and making configuration mistakes harder to catch.
evidence: index.d.ts:99-106 restricts rejectOnClear to readonly rejectOnClear?: boolean.
Focused runtime probe observed pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0}) was accepted.
findings.reproduction_or_test: Run pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0}); expected a TypeError for a non-boolean option, observed successful construction.

Graph was used for orientation only due search/recovery warnings and unrelated scan noise.
